title: Insuring Maturing Whisky Stock | Craft Beer School
desc: What a policy on maturing whisky should cover, how to value casks in a hot Indian warehouse and the questions to put to a broker.
teaser: Your most valuable asset sits in a shed full of flammable liquid for years. Here is how to think about insuring it.
standfirst: A young distillery can end up with more money in its warehouse than in its stills within a few years. Insuring that stock well means choosing a valuation basis, declaring it properly and knowing what no policy will pay for.
sections: Your warehouse becomes the balance sheet

A malt distillery fills casks every week and sells none of that whisky for years. Each cask ties up grain, energy, labour, the cask itself and often a duty or bond liability. Fill 20 barrels a week for three years and you hold more than 3,000 casks, all of it ethanol in wood under one roof.

That is why insurance for maturing stock is a planning topic, not paperwork for the end of the build. Lenders and investors will ask about it. Our guide to whisky inventory planning shows how fast the cask count grows; the insurance question grows at the same rate.

We are distillers who work in data, not brokers or lawyers. What follows is the set of questions we would want answered before signing. A licensed insurance broker who knows spirits should do the actual placing.
Choose how a cask is valued before you choose a policy

The single biggest decision is the valuation basis, because it sets what a claim pays. The usual options are:

  • Cost of production. What it cost you to make the spirit and fill the cask. Simple to prove from your batch records, but it ignores the years of ageing already paid for.
  • Cost plus an ageing uplift. Production cost increased by an agreed amount for each year in wood.
  • Market or selling value. What the whisky would fetch. Closest to your real loss, hardest to agree with an insurer.

Work it through for one barrel. A 200 litre cask filled at 63.5% ABV holds 127 litres of pure alcohol (LPA). Put a cost on each LPA, add the cask and the filling labour, then decide what each year of maturation adds. Agree that formula in writing with the insurer so a claim does not become an argument about what a four year old cask is worth.
Fire and ethanol vapour drive the risk

Whisky at cask strength is flammable. A warehouse fire is the event every distillery insurer prices first. Expect questions about construction, distance between buildings, fire breaks, electrical fittings in zoned areas, sprinklers or drenchers, drainage that keeps burning spirit from running into the next building and how far the nearest fire service is.

Small layout choices matter. Spreading stock across two warehouses limits the loss from one fire. Keeping forklift charging and other ignition sources out of the cask store is basic but often missed. Our guide to designing a whisky warehouse for Indian heat covers the building itself. Flood, theft, malicious damage, earthquake and roof failure under monsoon rain are the other perils to list one by one with your broker.
What no policy will pay for

Some losses are part of making whisky. The angel's share is the obvious one. In Scotland around 2% a year is commonly quoted; in Indian heat the loss runs well above that. Insurers treat this evaporation as a normal process loss, not an insured event, so budget for it in the inventory model instead.

Slow leaks found at a routine stock check usually fall in the same bucket unless you can show a sudden, accidental cause. Spirit that tastes wrong because a cask was poor is a quality problem, not damage. Read the exclusions as carefully as the cover. The gap between what you lose and what a policy pays is where young distilleries get hurt.
Declarations, duty and the paperwork that makes a claim work

Most stock policies need regular declarations of what is in the warehouse. Under-declare and a claim may be cut in proportion. Over-declare and you pay premium for whisky you do not have. A cask management system that gives you LPA by warehouse, by fill year and by cask type makes this a report rather than a weekend of counting.

Bonded stock adds a layer. Spirit held in bond usually carries a duty or excise liability that the state may still pursue if stock is lost, depending on the rules and the evidence you can give. State rules vary and change, so ask your licensing adviser what happens to the duty on destroyed stock and make sure the policy wording matches that answer.
The other covers a distillery usually needs

Stock cover sits next to several others. Business interruption pays for lost income while you rebuild, which matters more for a distillery than for most firms because a fire can wipe out several years of future releases at once. Transit cover protects casks moving between sites and bottled goods heading to depots or export ports. Product liability and recall cover the bottled end. Machinery breakdown covers stills, boilers and pumps.

Your first step this week: export a list of every cask with fill date, volume, strength and LPA. Then write down, in one line each, how you would value a one year, three year and five year cask. Take both to a broker. If you cannot produce the list in an afternoon, fix your records before you buy any policy.
faqs: Does insurance cover the angel's share?
No. Evaporation during maturation is a normal process loss. Budget for it in your inventory plan rather than expecting a policy to pay.
How should maturing whisky be valued for insurance?
Common bases are cost of production, cost plus an agreed uplift for each year of ageing or market value. Agree the formula in writing with the insurer before a loss happens.
Is excise duty on destroyed bonded stock covered?
It depends on state rules and the policy wording. Ask a licensing adviser how your state treats duty on lost stock, then check the policy matches.
Should a distillery split stock between warehouses?
Spreading casks across separate buildings limits the loss from any single fire. Insurers usually look at it favourably.
